item.title: More on flexed Week 12 game at Cleveland
item.description: Plenty of factors involved
item.content:encoded:
This week, the NFL flexed the Las Vegas Raiders’ game at the Cleveland Browns on November 29 has been flexed into Sunday Night Football. Kickoff is set for 5:20 p.m. PT.

Here are some thoughts on the decision:

Not many choices:

It’s a bit surprisisng that a game featuring a 4-6 team against a 6-4 team would be selected to be moved into prime time on the final Sunday of November. But there there were few choices and it’s better a Drake Maye-less New England Patriots against the one-win Los Angeles Chargers, which was the original choice. Because there are five games in a Wednesday-Friday window, there were few choices. So, this was a top option.

Fernando mania:

There’s no doubt the fact that No. 1 overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza is now the Raiders’ starting quarterback was part of the appeal for NBC for this choice. There will be more more prime-time opportunities in his future.

A little love for the Browns:

The Browns are definitely part of the ideal for this flex as well. They are 6-4 and are currently in the playoff mix. The Dawg Pound will be alive in the Browns’ first Sunday night affair in five years.

No early start:

This game was originally slotted for a 10 a.m. West Coast start, The Raiders are 1-1 in that time slot this season, but traditionally has struggled. So, the later start time can’t hurt.

Weather could be issue:

It could be cold and rainy. The current forecast calls for low 40s and a chance of rain on the shores of Lake Erie.

Any more flexes this season?

Could the Raiders’ get awarded a second flex? There are not many chances. The Raiders do host the Denver Broncos in Week 15, but the scheduled prime-time games Sunday and Monday games don’t look like they will be moved. However, if the Raiders beat Denver this week, perhaps the Week 15 game could be flexed to Thursday night. But the deadline for that switch will be next Tuesday. There will be three stand-alone games on Sunday of Week 18 when the Raiders play at Kansas City and the Sunday night game is open as well. So, that final game may be the Raiders’ best chance for a second stand-alone game.

item.title: Cowboys roundtable discussion: Christian Parker, Christian McCaffrey, and Tennessee Titans
item.description: Here is our latest roundtable discussion on the Cowboys
item.content:encoded:
Every week, we gather to discuss the latest news about the Dallas Cowboys and seek our writer’s perspective on each headline. Welcome back to the roundtable. This week we have Jorge Guajardo, Dyllan Rivers, Tom Ryle and Sean Martin. 

Christian Parker’s defense surrendered a franchise-record 584 yards at home against San Francisco. Was this down to player exectuion of poor coaching from Parker?

Mike – The biggest responsibility falls squarely on Christian Parker here. Players have to execute, maintain their assignments and make tackles, but when your defense surrenders a franchise-record 584 yards and 46 points at home, that’s a complete failure of coaching.

Kyle Shanahan repeatedly exposed Dallas with misdirection, poor defensive positioning and mismatches that Parker simply had no answers for. Parker is being outcoached every week, and the decision to strip him of play-calling duties tells you everything about how badly things have gone.

Jorge – Both. Pairing a rookie DC with this roster is a bad combination, and the results show every week. From a player standpoint, watching the film there are some guys not playing through the whistle, with some jogging while players appeared to be still in the mix.

As for Parker, he’s in way over his head, just like his head coach. Now, I think something needs to be said for good coaching. I think good coaching gets you to hustle and finish every play. Good coaching arms you with the knowledge to take the right angles to stop a certain play; good coaching puts you in positions to succeed, but none of that is apparent on this defense. Yes, the players also have responsibility. So this is a result of a match made in hell with Parker and a poor defensive roster.

Tom – Really, that’s the only answer that makes sense. It’s a perfect storm of ineptitude and it is threatening to sink Dallas. There are some talented players on the defensive side of the ball, but a combination of misuse and not everyone shouldering their share of the load is nullifying it. And let’s not forget the role the head coach plays in the motivation arena. I don’t know what is going on in the locker room, but I can’t help but worry that Schottenheimer is on the verge of losing it – if he hasn’t already.

Sean – All the respect in the world to Von Miller, but this was on coaching. It’s being kind to only use the last three weeks as a sample size, but just in this stretch where the Cowboys are 1-2 against two losing teams and a 49ers team they let break records on them, the explosive plays allowed are outrageous. 

Look elsewhere around the NFL, and games are being decided by razor thin margins even between teams you might expect to have a little more of a gap. Explosive plays are earned through a clear, visible effort from coaches to put players in those positions. Christian Parker’s defense is the antithesis to this. Whenever an offense needs a huge play, even for a touchdown, they can get it. 

Dyllan – All of the above. Christian Parker can’t control Elijah Garcia and James Houston chasing down a phantom running back 40 yards the wrong direction instead of containing the Deebo Samuel reverse. But Parker can decide to not call a zero blitz in the most crucial moment of the game, leaving Von Miller one-on-one with Christian McCaffrey. The perfect blend of mediocrity and misery has found its way to the Cowboys defense.

How does Dallas continue allowing such explosive plays, and was having Von Miller covering McCaffrey one-on-one the most baffling defensive decision of the game?

Mike – For me, this comes down to poor coaching, dreadful defensive discipline and Christian Parker repeatedly putting his players in positions to fail. Having a  37-year-old Von Miller isolated against McCaffrey in coverage is baffling and the best example of my statement of Parker putting players in positions to fail, he has to take responsibility for allowing such a ridiculous mismatch. The Cowboys continually lose their assignments, take poor tackling angles and fail to communicate, but these are recurring problems that should be getting corrected on the practice field. When the same mistakes happen every week, it’s no longer just poor execution, it’s poor coaching.

Jorge – In a game where the Cowboys gave up three plays over 65 yards that all ended in TDs, it’s hard to say that this is where the game was lost. However, the offense had clawed back to within one score; it was a 2nd-and-9, and a stop gives you a chance. You would think that in a game where your defense has already given up two disastrously long plays, you wouldn’t ask your 37-year-old, pass-rushing specialist linebacker to cover a back like CMC in his prime, right? Wrong. 

That’s exactly what Christian Parker did. A lot of people have said it was just a great counter from Shanahan to route CMC right at Miller. My counter is they’re right. Shanahan is a great coach with an incredible feel for the game, its moments and his roster. Christian Parker is not. How are you not prepared for that alternative? There never seems to be any contingencies with this team, and it’s defense. They simply run what they run, fail because their plans never survive contact with the enemy, and they have nothing prepared for the possibility that their plans may not work. Parker left Miller out to dry.

Tom – It is beyond embarrassing how the Cowboys just let one or more players absolutely go off on them every week. The topic of Schottenheimer’s job security is a popular one, but the seat is far hotter under Parker. A well run team would likely write him off as a failed one-year experiment and start planning for the next DC. That would hardly be helpful for the players to have to go into the third new system in three years, but what is the point in prolonging the bleeding? 

Unfortunately, that part about a well run team really doesn’t apply for Dallas. Worse, there is no likelihood that is going to change.

Sean – Maybe we should have just known better to not have hope during another frantic fourth quarter comeback by the Cowboys, but for all the ones in the past that felt pointless and hollow, this one against the 7-1 49ers actually felt real. The offense earned back a legitimate chance to retake the lead down by six, the comeback had legs. Then in the blink of an eye, McCaffrey is literally running so free that a Dallas defender couldn’t even dream of touching him. There was a 0% chance to make a tackle on that play, zero. 

It was sickening, inexcusable, and to answer your question, yes the most baffling decision of the game.

Dyllan – I don’t believe having Von Miller man up against Christian McCaffrey is something the 31 other defensive coordinators in the NFL would ever dream of doing, especially in clutch time. As far as the other explosives, it’s coming from a blend of losing the schematic chess match, poor tackling, and players simply making bad decisions. The fundamentals are missing for the second year in a row. The explosives will continue for as long as the most basic elements of defense are lost.

Tennessee enters this game with just one victory all season. Is anything less than a convincing Dallas victory unacceptable, and would losing to the Titans effectively end the Cowboys’ season?

Mike – Absolutely. Anything less than a convincing victory against Tennessee would be deeply concerning, and losing this game should effectively end any serious conversation about Dallas making the playoffs. Brian Schottenheimer needs to have this team prepared, aggressive and ready to take control early. More importantly, the defense must finally show it can handle an opponent without surrendering ridiculous explosive plays.

Jorge – The Cowboys will almost certainly make this a game, as they did against Indianapolis. The defense can only play solid for an entire half, so expect this to go down to the wire. Tennessee is not in the business of winning football games this year; I mean, neither are the Cowboys, although there is an illusion of it, but that’s a different story. That said, if the Cowboys lose to Tennessee on Sunday, the season is over, and the staff will pay with their jobs come season’s end. What a terrible season.

Tom – To your last question, yes, it would be the effective end of things. I just don’t see this team as having the resiliency to come back from that level of embarrassment, and while I agree that they will probably win, it is not a given. 

So we may see the flickering hopes for making something out of this year resting on Parker/Mike Pettine figuring things out. That is not good. The play-calling change change might shake things up and get a different fire lit under the players.

Sean – I don’t even want to slap a must win label on this one, because that also carries the connotation of a team building towards a goal by getting such wins, and the Cowboys don’t have that right now. They could win the next two and the only realistic take to have about it is that the team’s best case scenario is a repeat of last year, playing well through a stretch in November and that’s it. 

Even if they get these two wins, they would need one more to match last year’s win total and two to pass. The most likely two that Dallas can win are against their own division to end the season, and that’s just the worst sequel of all time at this point when it comes to not taking the bait over beating bad division opponents.

Beating the Titans would make Thanksgiving a little more enjoyable to not feel like absolutely all hope is lost by the holiday, but I think that’s about it.

Dyllan – Simply put, losing any more games against bad teams effectively ends the season. The “easy wins” need to be easy while Dallas also needs to steal potentially two out of three games against Jacksonville, Seattle, and the Rams. The Giants are helping the Cowboys stay alive, so Dallas needs to capitalize on the gift.

item.title: The Seahawks must put Drew Lock on the Russell Wilson plan
item.description: Drew Lock has outplayed Sam Darnold all season. With a bye week to decide, Mike Macdonald can do what Pete Carroll did in 2012 and give the job to the best quarterback, not the presumed starter.
item.content:encoded:
It’s interesting that the Seattle Seahawks first acquired Drew Lock in the Russell Wilson trade on March 8, 2022. That deal sent Wilson from Seattle to the Denver Broncos, along with a 2022 fourth-round draft pick, in exchange for Lock, tight end Noah Fant, defensive lineman Shelby Harris, 2022 and 2023 first-round picks, 2022 and 2023 second-round picks, and a 2022 fifth-round pick, and it set the Seahawks up for future success in ways few could have predicted at the time. Seattle got Devon Witherspoon, Charles Cross, Boye Mafe, and Derick Hall out of those picks, while Lock didn’t quite make the cut.

He was Geno Smith’s backup in 2022 and 2023, signed with the New York Giants for the 2024 season, and signed a two-year, $5 million deal to come back to the Emerald City in 2025. Not much came of it in 2025, as Sam Darnold had enough on the ball to help the Seahawks to their second Lombardi Trophy, but things have obviously been different in 2026. Darnold was injured early in the season opener against the New England Patriots, and Lock finished that 13-10 win, and a 31-7 Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals, looking very much like the NFL’s next reclamation quarterback. He completed 35 of 48 passes (72.9%) for 422 yards (8.8 yards per attempt), four touchdowns, no interceptions, a passer rating of 127.3 (the NFL’s highest among quarterbacks who took at least 20% of their teams’ snaps), and an EPA per pass of +0.43 (the NFL’s fourth-best).

Still, it made sense that a (relatively) healthy Darnold returned to the field in Week 3 against the Washington Commanders. Dan Quinn’s defense looked like an easy out, and the Lock story was more about the Seahawks having a top-tier backup than any sort of quarterback controversy. In that 33-31 upset loss, Darnold gave us the full Sam Darnold Experience, completing 31 of 45 passes for 379 yards, four touchdowns, two interceptions, a passer rating of 105.7, and an EPA per pass of +0.05.

Sam Darnold has lagged (far) behind.

From Week 4 through Week 8 as the starter, Darnold completed 95 of 164 passes (57.9%) for 1,086 yards (6.6 YPA), six touchdowns, seven interceptions, a passer rating of 72.4, and an EPA per pass of -0.18 — down there in the mid-thirties with Deshaun Watson, Cam Ward, Jalen Hurts, and Jacoby Brissett. Darnold’s injuries were clearly affecting him, and this was especially true when he tried to throw outside the pocket, which was a big factor in the Seahawks’ Super Bowl run. This season when throwing outside the pocket, Darnold has completed 13 of 35 passes for 162 yards, two touchdowns, one interception, a passer rating of 59.5, and an overall EPA of -12.14 — ninth-worst in the NFL.

Basically, because of his physical limitations, Darnold was put on a quick-game plan by offensive coordinator Brian Fleury — his average time to throw went from 3.14 seconds in Week 3 to 2.32 seconds in Week 7, and 2.67 seconds in Week 8.

I asked Darnold about this right after Seattle’s 34-17 Week 8 loss to the Chicago Bears — a game he finished despite a quadriceps injury and a cracked rib.

“Yeah, I think for me, it’s all about when I get the ball out quick,” he said. “It’s all about knowing where to go with the football. And I think, again, just being decisive, knowing when I need to move on in the progression and doing that. Talking about this game specifically, you gotta watch the tape, obviously, but I feel like there were opportunities to get the ball out, and I just didn’t.”

Fair enough, but when your passing game is that limited, it’s a problem. Especially when your run game has been behind the sticks all season long.

So, Lock was back under center for Seattle’s 17-3 Week 9 win over the Arizona Cardinals, and last Sunday’s 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders, and the work was similarly strong. In those two games, Lock completed 33 of 45 passes (73.3%) for 415 yards (9.2 YPA), three touchdowns, no interceptions, a passer rating of 123.8 (fourth-best in the NFL), and an EPA per pass of +0.22 (fifth-best).

Now, we have this to deal with.

Drew Lock gives the Seahawks the best chance to win.

By the way, Lock’s EPA per pass of +0.33 is the NFL’s highest among quarterbacks with at least 50 dropbacks. And he’s the quarterback who allows the Seahawks to run their entire offense at this point in time. Whether Darnold’s issues are tied to injuries and/or other things, he’s not able to do that right now.

Others have noticed.

“Oh my gosh, yeah,” Mike Macdonald said of Lock’s two touchdown passes out of scrambles against the Raiders. “He’s got that ability to extend plays and not put the ball in danger, which is cool. We turned it over twice, but those were really early in the play. Great plays, man. It was awesome.”

“Yeah, we just talked about creating plays,” Jaxon Smith-Njigba said after the Raiders game. “Drew’s a creative player, great player, can move around, great athleticism. So, just sticking with him, knowing that his eyes are downfield trying to make a play. Just being there for him.”

What Smith-Njigba said of Lock in the wake of Darnold’s possible return revealed even more.

“Man — unbelievable player, great player. Not only how he played incredibly, but just what he does off the field and in the huddle and how he commands his troops. True professional, and [I] love sharing the field with him.”

And how about an endorsement from Devon Witherspoon?

“Ah man, it’s dope. See Drew come out there and do the things he does. We watch him in practice all the time. I call him the Locksmith, because it seems like he’s just got all the damn coverages. To see Drew play the way he’s played, given the situation he’s in, you can’t ask for anything better than that. He comes out here and he works every day. We see the looks that we give every day in practice, man.

“We’ve got all the confidence in the world, because we know he put in the work to do it.”

By the way, Lock has done all this with injuries to his throwing elbow and his oblique muscles.

The best man must prevail.

Okay. What do I mean when I say in the headline that the Seahawks need to put Lock on the Russell Wilson plan? Let’s take a trip in the Wayback Machine.

I started covering the Seahawks with credentials in 2010, which means that I got to see the genesis of the Pete Carroll plan, and the creation of the Legion of Boom. I also got to see what happened in 2012 after the team signed Matt Flynn to a three-year, $19.5 million contract with $10 million guaranteed, and selected Russell Wilson with the 75th overall pick in the third round of that draft.

Wilson made his supremacy at the position evident from the start. At his rookie minicamp, he was making bang-on throws 40 yards downfield. As training camp turned into the preseason, I started hearing from veterans on the team that Wilson was the quarterback they trusted. He was the one they wanted to load the wagon behind. And that eventually happened, because Carroll understood the value of momentum, and that the best player must win the job, regardless of position.

Macdonald has said all the right things publicly about Darnold as his starter. But he’s also smart enough to know that with his team outside the playoff picture right now at 6-4, and a bye week to get everyone on the same page, this would be the ideal time to make the right call.

And regardless of the reasons why, the right call is to give Drew Lock all the starter’s reps. The difference in performance has been all the difference.

item.title: Bills Week 11 Power Rankings: Do power rankings matter heading into a divisional game?
item.description: Buffalo Bills Week 11 Power Rankings: Do power rankings matter heading into a divisional game?
item.content:encoded:
Despite a convincing win over the New York Jets, national analysts remain divided on whether Buffalo deserves the NFL’s top spot. The Buffalo Bills walked out of MetLife Stadium with a 31-12 victory over the New York Jets, but apparently a 19-point divisional win isn’t enough to impress everyone.

Heading into Week 11, Buffalo remains firmly entrenched among the NFL’s elite, with four of our eight tracked national outlets ranking the Bills No. 1 and the remaining four placing them at No. 2.

Interestingly, two outlets moved Buffalo in opposite directions following Sunday’s victory. ESPN dropped the Bills from first to second, while Sports Illustrated bumped them from third to second.

The result? Buffalo’s average ranking remained exactly where it was last week: 1.50.

While national analysts might disagree about which team deserves the top spot, there’s little disagreement that the Bills belong in the conversation.

Buffalo Bills Week 11 Power Rankings

ESPN drops Buffalo despite another convincing victory

Perhaps the most interesting development this week came from ESPN, which moved Buffalo from No. 1 to No. 2 following its victory over New York. It’s not as though the Bills struggled to put points on the board. Buffalo scored 31 points, generated 389 yards of offense, and kept the Jets out of the end zone entirely.

Was it a flawless performance? Absolutely not. The Bills converted just two of their 10 third-down opportunities, and the defense allowed New York to sustain several extended possessions.

However, Buffalo also produced three second-half touchdown drives totaling just seven plays and 2:49 of possession. 

James Cook rushed for 157 yards, including a 74-yard touchdown, while DJ Moore contributed 90 receiving yards and a score. Buffalo found ways to win comfortably without needing everything to go perfectly.

Power rankings aren’t simply about the previous week’s final score. Analysts consider the overall body of work, strength of opponents, and how teams stack up against other contenders.

Still, dropping a team after a 19-point divisional victory certainly raises some eyebrows.

USA Today FINALLY showing Buffalo some respect

Now here’s an outlet we’ve been watching closely. USA Today hasn’t exactly been Buffalo’s biggest supporter throughout the season. In fact, the Bills sat at No. 9 entering Week 8 before beginning a steady climb.

The Bills moved from No. 9 to No. 6 entering Week 9, then made an impressive four-spot jump from No. 6 to No. 2 heading into Week 10. FINALLY, some respect!

Following Buffalo’s victory over the Jets, USA Today kept the Bills at No. 2 for Week 11.

While USA Today isn’t quite ready to crown the Bills the NFL’s best team, the steady climb suggests Buffalo has done enough to change the perception of its overall performance.

And considering how long we’ve been watching USA Today rank Buffalo lower than several other national outlets, seeing the Bills maintain their place near the top is certainly worth acknowledging.

Miami Dolphins: A very different power rankings conversation

While Buffalo continues battling for the top spot in the national rankings, its next opponent finds itself at the opposite end of the conversation.

The Miami Dolphins enter Week 11 with considerably less confidence from national analysts.

USA Today dropped Miami five positions, from No. 27 to No. 32, while FOX Sports also placed the Dolphins last in its rankings. ESPN, NFL.com, and CBS Sports each ranked Miami No. 30.

It’s a striking contrast between two AFC East rivals heading into their Week 11 matchup. Buffalo is receiving serious consideration as the best team in football. Miami is being evaluated among the league’s worst.

However, divisional games have a way of making power rankings feel irrelevant once the ball is kicked off. The Bills cannot afford to overlook Miami simply because national analysts have little confidence in the Dolphins’ current trajectory.

The Bills remain among the NFL’s elite

Buffalo has an opportunity to continue building momentum, and another convincing divisional victory would only strengthen its case among the NFL’s top contenders. 

The biggest remaining question isn’t whether Buffalo belongs among the NFL’s elite. The national rankings have largely settled that debate. It’s whether the Bills can continue proving they deserve to be considered the very best.

With the struggling Dolphins coming to Buffalo, the Bills have another opportunity to make their case.

item.title: Inside the looming chess match between Kyle Shanahan and Brian Flores this weekend
item.description: Kyle Shanahan and the 49ers offense have their toughest test of the year.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are back in primetime on Sunday night, as they’re taking on the Minnesota Vikings in a battle between Top NFC contenders.

San Francisco, sitting at 8-1, is coming off a 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys, where its offense was unstoppable, while the defense had a ton of holes. Minnesota, on the other hand, just traded for Kirk Cousins at the trade deadline and blew out the Green Bay Packers in his first game back.

While Minnesota’s offense has raised questions this year, it’s the defense that has remained elite under coordinator Brian Flores, who has continued to find different ways for his defense to excel. This year, it’s with a blitz-heavy approach.

Flores has been able to neutralize teams all year long. No team has scored more than 25 points against the Vikings, and that lofty defense was what propelled Minnesota while its offense was struggling.

Flores has had head coach Kyle Shanahan’s number in the chess match between play-callers over the past few years. Regardless of the circumstances of the previous matchups, this is a perfect opportunity for Shanahan and the 49ers to establish themselves in many ways. It would continue to provide a boost in the NFC race, while also giving Shanahan another game to bolster his Coach of the Year case.

But Shanahan acknowledged the difficulty that Flores and his game plan will provide on Sunday.

“He just, he does it. He’s more unique than all the other 31 guys,” Shanahan said of Flores. “He’s the one guy who commits to this and it’s not just a fad for these nine games or whatever. He’s been doing it his whole time in Minnesota. He did the same thing in Miami. He’s as good as it gets at that stuff. Anybody who lives in that world as much as he does, it’s usually a matter of time.

“I think offensive coaches used to like to say that early on, but it’s too many years of it, and it’s too many games in this year that they’re sound. They put so much pressure on the quarterback, the play caller, the O-Line, the receivers, on everybody. A lot of times, when you go into an NFL game, the pressure’s really on people on third down and stuff like that because those are things where everything can come and when you play against Brian, it’s 70-straight plays of that.”

One position that Flores’s defenses have done really well to neutralize is the tight end position because of how much the Vikings blitz, forcing another blocker to stay in-line. That’s critical with Mike Evans currently not trending to play, leaving George Kittle as the team’s top weapon.

But overall, this game will be a chess match between the two brilliant minds who have arguably been the best play callers in the NFL this season. And there’s a lot on the line on both sides with the NFC race heating up.

item.title: Struggling Colts should start Anthony Richardson Sr. at QB the rest of the 2026 campaign
item.description: The consensus among Indianapolis Colts fans seems to be that this current rendition of Daniel Jones should no longer be the starting quarterback for the franchise. After leading the Colts to an 8-2 start last year, at the helm of a historically elite offense at the time, the wheels have quickly come off for Jones […]
item.content:encoded:
The consensus among Indianapolis Colts fans seems to be that this current rendition of Daniel Jones should no longer be the starting quarterback for the franchise.

After leading the Colts to an 8-2 start last year, at the helm of a historically elite offense at the time, the wheels have quickly come off for Jones and the franchise. Cracks of vulnerability were beginning to show even before Jones suffered critical injuries late last season, including a fractured fibula and season-ending torn Achilles. Most notably, opposing defenses began to blitz Jones at a higher rate, and started having a greater deal of success.

Jones continues to be pass pressured at a high rate, and while there may be some expected physical limitations, still working his way back less than a year removed from the torn Achilles, Jones’ regression doesn’t appear to be all physical—as his mental processing and decision-making in-game has also relapsed. He much more closely resembles the turnover prone former failed franchise quarterback hopeful for the New York Giants, than the breakout Pro Bowler that Colts fans saw firsthand for the first half of the 2025 campaign.

Embattled Colts head coach Shane Steichen values the much maligned Jones’ continued leadership, preparation, and understanding of the offense, but his on-the-field production so far this season for the 3-7 Colts stinks:

  • Completion rate: 59.6 (28th)
  • Passing yards: 1,830 (19th)
  • Yards Per Attempt: 5.6 (31st)
  • Yards Per Catch: 9.5 (29th)
  • Interceptions: 12 (1st most)
  • Sacks: 25 (6th most)
  • EPA per play: -0.173 (30th)

ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler recently reported that Steichen sticking with Jones, despite his continued struggles, may speak more to the lack of viable quarterback options behind him:

Colts head coach Shane Steichen’s loyalty to Daniel Jones might be less about Jones’ poor performance and more about the options behind him. As it was told to me, Steichen simply is not motivated to play Anthony Richardson Sr., the 2023 fourth overall pick who fell out of favor after a strong start to his rookie year. Richardson and No. 3 quarterback Riley Leonard did not have strong training camps in the Colts’ view, and it seems that has carried over. Richardson, a 2027 free agent, badly needs a fresh start elsewhere but appears poised for spot duty in Indy at some point this year, given the team’s 3-7 record and its trading away of four key players before the deadline. But I just don’t see Steichen benching Jones right now unless absolutely necessary.

That being said, if Steichen doesn’t believe that Richardson can even supplant this clearly spiraling version of Jones, then what was the point of even keeping him on as the primary backup? They should’ve just moved him.

Furthermore, even if Richardson Sr. didn’t have a particularly strong 2026 training camp, neither did Jones in 2025 Colts training camp when he won the starting job from Richardson Sr. and was named the new starter just weeks before the regular season started.

If anything, Richardson Sr. was arguably the stronger on-the-field performer in 2025 camp, whereas Jones won the job because of his off the field study and practice habits, and mental understanding of Steichen’s offense.

I’m not saying Richardson Sr. is going to be the savior either, but at the very least, he could potentially provide this stalling passing offense a much needed spark, especially with his big arm and willingness to throw the ball downfield—which at the very least, is more exciting offense than the “Charlie Checkdown” Jones we’ve seen.

For a team on a short week missing its two starting offensive tackles, and facing Houston Texans All-Pro pass rusher Will Anderson Jr. on Thursday night, Richardson Sr. could also provide much needed mobility and escapability in the passing pocket, while making the Colts ground game more dynamic and versatile, and harder to defend and predict for the opposing defense.

Coming off the Achilles, this current version of Jones hasn’t looked nearly as explosive or comfortable running with the football, so Richardson Sr.‘s improved mobility would be a significant upgrade in that regard.

I’m just having a tough time with this one because Jones starting for the 2026 Colts has clearly run its course, and it’s hard to see how starting Richardson Sr. could be any worse. The status quo at QB isn’t working.

At the very least too, it provides the Colts, who are clearly going nowhere fast, one last extended look at the 24-year-old Richardson Sr., to see if he’s made any significant jumps in passing accuracy and progression of reads, and safely close the chapter on his time here—should he falter again.

item.title: Bill Belichick, Robert Kraft one step closer to Pro Football Hall of Fame induction
item.description: The Patriots will be well-represented in the final rounds of Hall of Fame voting.
item.content:encoded:
Two key members of the New England Patriots dynasty are a step closer to Pro Football Hall of Fame induction.

Former head coach Bill Belichick and team owner Robert Kraft have been selected by the Hall of Fame’s respective coach and contributor subcommittees as candidates for induction in 2027.

They are now among 15 total candidates, who are up for the final voting rounds in February. They will be joined by 13 as-of-yet-unannounced players at a later point.

Belichick, 74, emerged from a group of five coaching nominees, beating out the likes of Tom Coughlin, Mike Holmgren, Dan Reeves and Mike Shanahan.

A six-time Super Bowl champion as New England’s head coach, who also earned two rings as defensive coordinator with the New York Giants, he won a combined 69% 0f regular season and playoff games between 2000 and 2023 and earned nine conference championships and 17 division titles. Including a previous head-coaching tenure with the Browns, he ranks second all-time in NFL coaching wins with 333 and first with 31 postseason victories; he also is a member of the NFL’s 100th Anniversary Team

Seemingly a lock to make the Hall of Fame based on his unrivaled résumé, Belichick was denied the honor of first-ballot induction last year in what is arguably the most controversial decision in the Hall of Fame’s history. His exclusion from the 2026 class drew heavy criticism and set the stage for the implementation of sweeping changes to the selection process.

Kraft, 85, garnered the subcommittee’s support over fellow contributor nominees Ralph Hay, Virginia McCaskey, Doug Williams and John Wooten.

His ownership saw the Patriots turn from a relative afterthought into the NFL’s most successful franchise. Besides winning six Super Bowls and reaching two others, he also oversaw 20 AFC East titles, 23 playoff berths, and only six losing seasons. The club has sold out every home game since he bought it in 1994, and won a combined 66% of games along the way.

To make it into the Hall of Fame, Belichick and Kraft will need to garner at least 80% of votes from the full selection committee at its next meeting ahead of the Super Bowl. The group will first be reduced from 15 to 10, with between three and seven finalists ultimately receiving the honor.

The expectation is that former Patriots tight end Rob Gronkowski will join them among the 15 candidates.

item.title: NFL predictions: Our picks for Giants-Jaguars, the full Week 11 slate
item.description: BBV staff isn’t confident in the Giants this week.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants face major test this week when they face the Jacksonville Jaguars. It is also a game that will provide a huge swing in the Giants’ expected chances to make the playoffs. Will the Giants upset Jacksonville? See what our Big Blue View staff members think about that game and the rest of the Week 11 action in this week’s staff picks.

View Link

Chris Pflum

I don’t think the Giants win this game.

I think there’s a path to a win for the Giants, if they can find it. The Giants are one of the very best teams in the NFL at forcing drives to end in punts. At the same time, the Jaguars will be without their starting center and the Giants are one of the best teams in the League at creating quick pressure. That’s important because Trevor Lawrence has been one of the quarterbacks most affected by pressure in the NFL.

At the same time, the Giants have rediscovered the explosive pass with J.J. McCarthy, which has been the weakness of the Jags’ defense.

If the Giants can score touchdowns while disrupting Lawrence, they’ve got the chance to come away with the upset. We’ve seen the Giants rebound after bad games, as well as play much better than anticipated when they’re underdogs. Maybe both will happen here.

The flip side of the coin is simpler and scarier to me: The Giants have one of the worst red zone defenses in the NFL, and the Jaguars have one of the best red zone offenses in the league. If the Giants can’t stop them between the 20s, this game could get ugly fast.

Pick: Jaguars

Nick Falato

Jacksonville is one of the hottest teams in the league with a young and explosive offense that can run the football. Their defense is aggressive but doesn’t NEED to bring the blitz — they blitz at about a league-average rate, but Anthony Campanile does an excellent job utilizing simulated pressure to harass opposing quarterbacks. Jacksonville is third in offensive EPA, 4th in defensive EPA allowed, and 1st in Net EPA — they’re a juggernaut based on their performance and the advanced analytics.

Still, that doesn’t mean the Giants don’t have a chance — they just must play efficient football and avoid the catastrophic mistakes that have robbed them of wins. It’s possible, but against the most efficient team in the NFL, it will be difficult. John Harbaugh will have the Giants ready and prepared for the game, and I believe it will be more exciting and competitive. Jacksonville is concluding their third straight road game, which could give the Giants a slight advantage at home, but I ultimately believe the better team finds a way to win.

Pick: Jaguars

David Hartman

It took 11 weeks, but for the first time this season, the Giants will face a team with a winning record when the 7-2 Jaguars come to town on Sunday. Not only is Jacksonville running away with the AFC South (they lead the division by four games), but they’re steamrolling the competition. They’ve won their last three games by a combined 75 points. This is easily Big Blue’s toughest test of the season, so far.

Jacksonville is very good on both sides of the ball. They’re fourth in offensive DVOA, third in defensive DVOA, and third in overall DVOA. They also have an excellent field goal kicker with crazy range. If you look at both rosters, it’s hard to find clear advantages for the Giants at any position group outside of tight end, and even there, Jacksonville has good players.

Can the Giants win this game? Yes. They’re at home, they’re getting an extra three days of rest, and as we saw when they played Houston, they aren’t scared and can surprise as a big underdog. They’ll need to dial it up on defense and pressure Trevor Lawrence into the kinds of mistakes he used to make before Liam Coen got there. They also might have a little extra motivation after letting last week’s game against the Commanders slip away at the end.

I won’t be surprised if John Harbaugh’s team hangs in there and keeps it as a one-score game most of the way. But in the end, until the Giants show me that they can beat a really good team, I can’t pick them to do so.

Pick: Jaguars

Tony Del Genio

You can talk yourself into believing that the Giants can beat Jacksonville this Sunday. They needed a miraculous last-second 57-yard field goal to beat the Eagles team (with Jalen Hurts) that the Giants defeated (without Hurts). They lost to the Texans team that the Giants beat the following week. The woeful Titans were within a TD against them last week with 5 minutes left. So indeed, it could be a competitive game. Unfortunately, the Jags have also won games by 24, 29, 35, and 23 points this season. They have scored 31 or more in each of their past four games, and over 40 in two of those. The Giants have only scored more than 30 points once, and only then because of a 99-yard pick-6 on the last play of the game.

Trevor Lawrence isn’t necessarily playing any better this year than in the past. He’s a QB that simultaneously makes great passes and puts the ball up for grabs, yet unlike in years past, he’s cut down on the INTs while getting the TDs. Part of that may be due to 5’10” wide receiver Parker Washington (a 2023 6th-round pick), who had a breakout 2025 and is on pace for 1,000 yards. Running back Bhayshul Tuten, a 4th round 2025 pick, isn’t quite in the Jahmyr Gibbs – Kenneth Walker class but he’s not far below and is a missed tackle machine. A lot of the credit has to go to head coach Liam Coen, who also calls the plays and turned this team around as soon as he was hired. Lawrence, like most QBs, has trouble with pressure, but he is not too fazed by the blitz. Finding a way to disrupt his rhythm is a key to any chance the Giants may have.

On defense, the Jaguars are strong at linebacker with fourth-round 2023 pick Ventrell Miller, one of the league’s best (note how many mid-round picks the Jags have hit on), along with Foyesade Oluokun. They also put on a decent pass rush with Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker, and Dennis Gardeck. In the secondary, Travis Hunter is playing more like a No. 2 pick, having mostly given up his evening gig as a receiver.

Are the Giants a serious playoff contender? This is the type of game they can use to make a statement against a team that is in the Super Bowl conversation. I think they’ll put up a fight. I also don’t think they’re there yet.

Pick: Jaguars

Valentine’s View

I want to convince myself to pick the Giants to defeat the Jaguars. I really do. I just can’t. The Jaguars are a team with justifiable Super Bowl ambitions. They are a well-rounded team with a high-powered offense, a very good defense, and one of the best field-goal kickers in the business in Cam Little.

The Giants are a good team. They are resilient. They will give the Jaguars their best shot. Maybe, just maybe, it will be good enough to pull off an upset that would go a long way toward ensuring that the Giants make the playoffs.

I just can’t pick them to do it.

Pick: Jaguars

item.description: Denver Broncos cornerback Riley Moss's contract was due to expire after 2026. See the details on the new deal keeping him in Denver.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos have established slightly more stability to the future of their secondary.

Cornerback Riley Moss is signing a four-year, $67 million extension with the team that drafted him, according to multiple reports. Moss was one of six defensive backs – and one of three members of the secondary at the top of the depth chart – poised to hit free agency after the 2026 season. Now, he's set to stay in Denver through 2030.

The Iowa product was a third-round pick by the Broncos in the 2023 NFL Draft. The 2026 season, Moss's fourth, was the final year of his rookie contract.

RAIDERS AT BRONCOS: Predictions, picks and odds for NFL Week 11 game

Through eight games this year, Moss is on pace for a second solid season in a row. Last year, he tied for the NFL lead with 19 passes defended, per Pro Football Reference. Moss also recorded his second career interception last year and his first career sack. In 2026, Moss already has an interception, along with eight passes defended in eight games.

Moss has missed six games due to injury in his career, including Week 5 this year with a rib injury. He also suffered a concussion in Week 9 that kept him out of the second half. He's not expected to miss any additional time after Denver's Week 10 bye.

Here's what to know about Moss's new contract:

Riley Moss contract details

Here are the terms of the fourth-year cornerback's contract extension, according to reports.

  • Term: Four years
  • Total value: $67 million
  • Average annual value (AAV): $16.75 million
  • Guaranteed money: TBA

Moss is getting a significant pay bump from the four-year, $5.44 million deal he signed before his rookie year. The AAV of his extension with the Broncos is bigger than the total value of his initial contract.

According to Over The Cap, the Moss extension will rank 16th among NFL cornerbacks in total value, above the Browns' Denzel Ward but below Bills CB Christian Benford. Moss's deal also comes out to 23rd among NFL cornerbacks in AAV, between Rams' Jaylen Watson ($17 million/year) and Buccaneers' Zyon McCollum ($16 million/year).

Riley Moss stats

Moss has missed the second half of Weeks 4 and 9 with rib and head injuries, respectively. He also missed Week 5 while still dealing with his rib ailment.

Here's how his stats look through eight games in 2026:

  • Games (starts): 8 (8)
  • Tackles: 27
  • Passes defended: 8
  • Interceptions: 1

Moss also has the second-highest missed-tackle rate in the league among cornerbacks with more than 400 snaps played this year (27.8%). His teammate, Ja'Quan McMillian, is at the top: 33.3%.

item.title: Broncos sign CB Riley Moss to a four-year contract extension worth $67 million
item.description: According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero, the Denver Broncos are finalizing a four-year contract extension with cornerback Riley Moss. It is a four-year deal worth up to $67 million dollars as the Broncos lock up one of their key starters in their secondary. The story heading into the season was: which player would the Broncos […]
item.content:encoded:
According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero, the Denver Broncos are finalizing a four-year contract extension with cornerback Riley Moss. It is a four-year deal worth up to $67 million dollars as the Broncos lock up one of their key starters in their secondary.

The story heading into the season was: which player would the Broncos re-sign? Cornerback Riley Moss, whom the Broncos spent a 3rd-round pick on, or cornerback Ja’Quan McMillian, a former undrafted free agent this coaching staff inherited? Well, at least for now, it appears Moss is their choice. He signed a four-year extension, which makes him the 23rd highest-paid cornerback in the league right now.

While many wanted the team to re-sign Ja’Quan McMillian, and honestly, they may still, Moss is worthy of this extension. He has one of the hardest jobs in the NFL, which is playing opposite star cornerback Pat Surtain II. Teams avoid going after Surtain II, which means more targets go Moss’s way. Yes, he has had some struggles, and the refs, for whatever reason, love to call phantom penalties on him, but he has been a key part of the success of the Broncos’ secondary these past few years. Now, both he and Surtain II are locked up and will keep their secondary strong for the foreseeable future.

Now, all eyes go to star slot corner Ja’Quan McMillian. He remains a pending free agent next season, and the narrative always was that the Broncos will likely have to pick between him and Moss. Well, Moss has an extension, so was the decision made? Perhaps, but there is some room for optimism, in my opinion. Slot corners are typically cheaper than outside corners, and the struggles of Jahdae Barron recently could have the Broncos wanting to bring back both. With that said, you do have Jahdae Barron, a former first-round pick who profiles as a slot corner and someone who many assumed would take McMillian’s job when he was drafted. Could they still have faith in their first-round investment and risk letting McMillian walk?

We’ll see.

At the very least, the Broncos have Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss locked up for the foreseeable future, and that should keep the Denver Broncos’ secondary strong moving forward. We will just have to see what this Moss extensions means for Ja’Quan McMiillian and his future with the team.

item.title: Rams captain has blunt message for LA’s defense before Packers showdown
item.description: Trent McDuffie says the Rams must create more turnovers as injuries mount and Los Angeles prepares for a crucial NFC playoff showdown with the Packers.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams spent millions of dollars assembling a loaded defense in the offseason.

They signed an All-Pro cornerback in Trent McDuffie, acquired the reigning Defensive Player of the Year winner in Myles Garrett, and lured future Hall of Famer Aaron Donald out of retirement. 

Now, as they head into their bye week, just one week away from a primetime Thanksgiving Eve showdown with the Green Bay Packers, it would be a good time for that investment to start paying dividends.

Against Green Bay, and with their playoff hopes potentially hanging in the balance, the Rams can’t afford to just stop Jordan Love and the Packers’ offense, they need to create turnovers and McDuffie knows it. 

“Our defense is sitting somewhere in the 20s for turnover ratio,” McDuffie told The California Post in an exclusive interview. “So it’s a big mindset this week: turnovers, turnovers.”

He’s close. The Rams are currently tied for 16th in opponents’ turnovers in the NFL, and that’s before the rest of the league plays their Week 11 slate of games. 

But that message of needing to force turnovers carries even more weight heading into a nationally televised Thanksgiving Eve showdown between two teams tied for the NFC’s seventh and final playoff spot.

The winner would seize control of the head-to-head tiebreaker. The loser could find itself chasing not only victories but favors from other teams over the final stretch.

The Rams’ current injury crisis puts even more pressure on their defense heading into this crucial matchup. 

The Rams will take the field against Green Bay without star receivers Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, along with starting center Coleman Shelton. Left guard Steve Avila and tight end Terrance Ferguson are also dealing with hamstring injuries, leaving their availability uncertain.

The Rams’ offense has continued to find creative ways to replace those weapons, but if McDuffie, Garrett and Donald can help that offense with stops, sacks, turnovers, and field position, it could be the difference between making the playoffs and watching them from home come January. 

“W​​hether it’s picks, whether it’s forced fumbles, whether it’s turnovers on fourth down, whatever we can do to get the ball back to the offense and, like I said, produce this win,” McDuffie said.

McDuffie, whose 98.9 impact grade leads all NFL cornerbacks according to Pro Football Network, understands the difference between a good defense and one capable of changing a season.

“As a defense, we’re coming with the right mindset and attitude and understanding of what this game is,” said McDuffie. “We have a really good opportunity. Everybody’s kind of in this mode where it’s ‘fight for a win.’ And you’ve got to love being in those battles.”

The Rams’ defense is coming off a 34-6 victory over the Arizona Cardinals in which they held them to no touchdowns and just two field goals. They will need that performance to carry over against the Packers if they want to keep their playoff hopes alive. 

“This is a huge one for everybody,” McDuffie said.

item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions defense is going through some serious changes this week, whether they want to or not.

Losing Aidan Hutchinson for the season will create a ripple effect across the team’s defensive roster. Not only will that mean new opportunities for new players—see: Ahmed Hassanein—but Detroit will undoubtedly have to adjust how they approach their entire defensive scheme. Will they lean more on blitzing to make up for losses in the pass rush? Will they devote more resources to coverage, hoping that if receivers are blanketed a little longer, it can help the weakened pass rush get home?

Luckily for Detroit, Hutchinson’s exit coincides with the return of a key defensive piece: All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph. The Lions activated Joseph this week, and coach Dan Campbell indicated he’ll have a pretty significant role in his debut against the Buccaneers on Sunday. With Chuck Clark and Brian Branch playing well right now, could some three-safety looks help Detroit mitigate some of the damage left by Hutchinson’s injury?

That’s the big topic on this week’s Midweek Mailbag.

Note: This week’s episode was filmed before Campbell spilled the beans and told the media that Hassanein would make his debut this week. So some of our thoughts on him are outdated.

Other topics of discussion during this week’s show are:

  • How much of the defensive improvement over the last month is sustainable vs. how much was just poor offensive opponents?
  • Has Juice Scruggs officially Wally Pipp’d Cade Mays? And what should the Lions do with Scruggs this offseason?
  • Should there be concern about Sam LaPorta’s lack of production—and will that impact contract discussions?
  • Jahmyr Gibbs and Jaxon Smith-Njigba are trending towards record-breaking years: who will win Offensive Player of the Year if they both tear down the record books?

item.title: Seahawks All-22 Review: An unsung hero stands out in Raiders game
item.description: A strong defensive finish saved Seattle, but the first-half tape tells a different story.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks got the win, but there isn’t much to celebrate when you consider the level of competition against the Las Vegas Raiders. Still, this victory was important. It gives the Seahawks some breathing room heading into the bye week, allowing them to get healthy and prepare for the final stretch of the season.

There was good, there was bad, and there are still plenty of questions to answer.

Let’s get into the film.

The Bad

A defensive start that should raise concerns

The first half against the Raiders exposed some concerning issues with Mike Macdonald’s defense. Even against a rookie quarterback making his first career start, Seattle took far too long to make him uncomfortable. Context matters here: Las Vegas entered the game with the NFL’s 31st-ranked rushing offense, averaging just 71.3 yards per game. The Raiders also lost Brock Bowers, one of their most important offensive weapons, during the first half.

Fernando Mendoza completed his first seven passes. His first incompletion didn’t come until the second quarter. Seattle didn’t record its first sack until late in the first half, when Devon Witherspoon brought him down after Mendoza had already attempted 12 passes.

At halftime, the rookie was 11-of-13 for 90 passing yards, with 21 rushing yards and a rushing touchdown. He had no interceptions. To make matters worse, the Raiders converted seven of their ten third-down attempts, a 70% conversion rate.

One thing that helped Mendoza was Seattle’s tendency to overcommit to the run despite facing an offense with such poor rushing production. That opened the door for Klint Kubiak’s familiar play-action concepts, taking pressure off the quarterback and creating opportunities for the tight ends. On the play above, both tight ends end up wide open.

Fernando Mendoza pulled off one of the most memorable plays in College Football Playoff history with a quarterback draw in the national title game. Seattle wasn’t prepared for this look. The Raiders spread the defense out of an empty formation, forcing a man-coverage look. Murphy executes a stunt, but Reed is supposed to be the looper and fails to fulfill his assignment, making life easier for the offense as it attacks Ernest Jones. Okada also takes a poor angle and ends up getting screened by his own teammate.

One area I’ve found particularly concerning is Seattle’s intermediate coverage. The defense has repeatedly struggled against dig routes attacking the space behind the linebackers. Here, the Seahawks are bailed out by Derick Hall winning with pure power and getting to the quarterback.

The offensive line continues to have execution issues

If we assume Bradford has settled into a backup role, Seattle essentially played with three backup offensive linemen after Bobby Hart was forced into action. The offensive line continued to show recurring execution and communication problems.

Maxx Crosby adjusts his alignment before the snap, and the communication between Zabel and Jones breaks down. Crosby gets a free path into the backfield and makes the tackle. These issues with identifying pressure, adjusting protection, and coordinating assignments at the second level have become recurring problems.

Josh Jones doesn’t seem to recognize the play being called here. He initially blocks alongside Zabel before releasing to the second level as if this were a running play. That mistake wipes out what should have been a big reception for JSN.

Bobby Hart was thrown into a difficult situation, but considering his recent level of play, things could have been much worse. Once again, the Raiders use their pre-snap alignment changes to move Crosby around. Hart fails to adjust his angle and allows Crosby to penetrate the backfield.

As mentioned earlier, these aren’t just isolated individual mistakes. There are broader execution problems across the unit. Hart fails to create any movement and gets driven backward. Sundell climbs to the second level but gets caught between linebackers No. 7 and No. 17, ultimately blocking neither. Bradford also gets badly beaten, and the play ends in a tackle for loss. On the left side, Zabel and Jones don’t execute their assignments particularly well either.

It’s worth mentioning that there were some genuinely good run-blocking reps, even if they came against the Raiders. All three tight ends deliver excellent blocks, particularly Kallerup and Barner. Josh Jones seals the edge and even helps Zabel. Sundell delivers one of his best blocks of the season, climbing to the linebacker and taking him to the ground.

The Good

Brian Fleury: A mixed bag of results

This section is essentially a good-and-bad breakdown, because Fleury could easily appear in either category. The offensive coordinator was extremely conservative and methodical, failing to consistently challenge a bad defense in the first half. Seattle went into halftime with just seven points.

Route spacing continues to be a recurring issue. Watch where the receivers are positioned as Lock begins to leave the pocket. Kupp and Shaheed are occupying the middle of the field, while JSN and Barner are near the sideline. They’re effectively crowding the same areas and shrinking the quarterback’s options.

Here we get a look at a page from Klint Kubiak’s playbook: the Yankee concept. It’s a deep-shot play-action design featuring two vertical routes while the rest of the offense stays in protection. Kubiak used this concept frequently, but Fleury hasn’t shown the same willingness to call it.

JSN’s route is excellent, and the safety gets held in place by the threat of Shaheed. As for the alleged OPI: if this is offensive pass interference, Mike Evans, DeAndre Hopkins, and plenty of other receivers wouldn’t have the production they do.

Seattle has also been using JSN out of the backfield. The play design could be better, but aligning him there makes it harder for the defense to double-cover him and complicates the leverage and angles for defenders #3 and #31. The inside-breaking man-coverage routes should create space for JSN. And when he gets his one-on-one matchup, he does what he does best: wins and picks up the crucial first down.

This was easily one of the most encouraging plays of the game. Lock manipulates the Raiders’ defense, and Seattle clearly wants to run the ball in this situation. He keeps it, takes advantage of Crosby’s aggressive upfield rush, and finds a clear path to the first down. It’s reminiscent of Peyton Manning’s famous naked bootleg touchdown against the Cowboys.

Drew Lock had his own highs and lows

Lock may have made his first truly costly mistakes of the season, with two turnovers that had a direct impact on the game.

The defense doesn’t respect the play-action fake, and nobody bites. Instead, defenders immediately pursue the quarterback. Abe Lucas is slow to recognize the blitz, allowing a Raiders defender to pressure Lock. Shaheed is open on the dig route, with JSN creating space for his teammate.

Lock needs to climb the pocket, but it collapses around him. This is a situation where he simply needs to eat the sack and move on to the next play. It’s the opening drive; there’s no reason to force something. This was the most Sam Darnold-esque play possible.

Not long after his first turnover, Lock delivers a huge touchdown. The play design is questionable for a long third down, with the routes initially breaking well short of the sticks.

Lock buys time, and this is where you see the importance of Kupp’s mentality. He never gives up on the play, while No. 5 momentarily does. Lock keeps his eyes downfield, resists the temptation to scramble, and eventually delivers the long touchdown.

This appears to be the same concept Seattle used on the touchdown against the Chargers. It’s a heavy formation, and the quarterback should have the option to throw to Horton. The receiver is running an option route between a fade and a slant.

This should have been a touchdown, but Lock’s dropback is too far and Charbonnet’s action aren’t synchronized. Seattle misses the opportunity and ends up committing its second turnover.

This is a good play call on third-and-three. The Raiders appear to be playing a Tampa 2-Invert look, which they had shown several times earlier.

Lock has JSN available for the first down, with Shaheed sitting a little deeper. However, JSN slips, and Lock holds onto the ball. The receiver improvises and ends up isolated against a linebacker in space, an ideal matchup.

The QB delivers an excellent throw, understanding that the linebacker cannot afford to turn his back and look for the ball. Doing so would be fatal to the coverage.

The defense finally found its rhythm

Seattle’s defense responded much better after halftime. After allowing 136 net yards in the first half, the Seahawks limited the Raiders to just 27 net yards after the break. They recorded four sacks, forced five three-and-outs, and held Las Vegas to 0-for-7 on third down.

The pass rush finally started making Mendoza uncomfortable, taking away his ability to operate freely and making it much harder for the Raiders to sustain drives.

The one major blemish was a significant coverage bust. In the fourth quarter, Mendoza found Ashton Jeanty on a short pass over the middle, and the running back turned it into a 38-yard gain, all the way to Seattle’s 15-yard line. That single play accounted for more yardage than the Raiders’ entire net offensive production in the second half. Remove that gain, and Las Vegas finishes the half with negative 11 net yards.

Seattle’s run defense showed a very different level of discipline. Murphy wins his matchup quickly, and Nick Emmanwori, who had an outstanding game, isn’t displaced by the tight end. He disengages, adjusts his angle, and makes the immediate tackle without allowing extra yards, with Ernest Jones aggressively closing in as well.

Seven defenders show along the line of scrimmage. Seattle drops its defensive tackles into the middle of the field, a Mike Macdonald staple designed to take away the short passing windows while giving the free rusher—in this case, Fowler—time to get home.

Okada also works as a late blitzer after Michael Mayer stays in to block.

For me, this was Macdonald’s best defensive call of the game. Seattle showed this overload blitz to one side of the formation several times, including on the snap discussed above. The idea is to force the offensive line to slide toward the side showing the most threats.

But the pressure actually comes from the opposite side, with Spoon doing an excellent job disguising his intentions. Nobody picks up Witherspoon, while the five offensive linemen are left dealing with the two defensive tackles attacking the interior gaps and creating a free path for the blitz.

It’s not unusual to see Spoon used as a blitzer. What is unusual is seeing him come from an outside alignment rather than his usual nickel position. That catches the offensive line—and even the running back, who is supposed to provide additional protection—completely off guard.

Another excellent job disguising the pressure before the snap.

An unsung hero: Nick Kallerup’s impact goes beyond the box score

I wanted to use this section to highlight Kallerup’s work. He finished the game injured, and the snap above appears to show something around his ankle. According to Mike Macdonald, however, it wasn’t anything serious.

His impact doesn’t show up in the box score. This play would have been an opportunity for him to make a statistical contribution, but Lock went with his first and safer read, Barner.

He’s crucial in helping Barner initially handle Crosby (Barner executes the block very well). Kallerup then works outside, drives his defender backward, and creates space for the running back to gain yardage.

He does something similar to what he did on Emmanuel Wilson’s touchdown against the Chiefs. He helps take down the defensive tackle before continuing to look for work, climbing to linebacker Quay Walker and creating a running lane for a solid gain.

Final Thoughts

It wasn’t a pretty win, and it certainly wasn’t a mistake-free performance. The opponent was weak, so ultimately the most important thing was getting the victory and heading into the bye week with some breathing room to recover injured players and prepare for the final stretch.

The next game against the San Francisco 49ers is arguably the defining matchup of the season. A loss would essentially eliminate Seattle’s remaining hopes of winning the division and make the Wild Card race considerably more difficult.

The focus now has to be on using the bye week properly. We have the blueprint for making life miserable for a rookie quarterback, but the first-half issues we saw against the Raiders could become much more costly against better teams.

Go Hawks!

item.title: Snubbed Bill Belichick a Pro Football Hall of Fame finalist again
item.description: Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft, who won six Super Bowls together with the Patriots, are back in the final round of Hall of Fame voting. Here's what's next.
item.content:encoded:
Here we go again.

Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft, who won six Super Bowls together with the New England Patriots, have advanced a step closer to reuniting in Canton as members of the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s Class of 2027.

Both were denied earlier this year for the Hall’s most recent class, and in the case of Belichick – a first-ballot finalist in 2026 and second to Don Shula for most career coaching victories (333) – the omission ignited a furor that prompted the Hall of Fame to overhaul its selection process.

Now they are back in the mix for a final round, with Belichick advancing over four others – Tom Coughlin, Mike Holmgren, Dan Reeves and Mike Shanahan (in alphabetical order) – in voting by the coaches subcommittee.

Kraft – one of the NFL’s most powerful and accomplished team owners, and a key figure in striking massive media rights deals for the league and in negotiating the collective bargaining agreement with players that ended a lockout in 2011 – was forwarded again as the candidate in the contributor category. He was chosen over four others – Ralph Hay, Virginia McCaskey, Doug Williams and John Wooten (in alphabetical order) – by a separate contributors subcommittee.

What next for Bill Belichick Hall of Fame bid?

The Hall’s full selection committee will consider Belichick and Kraft as part of a slate that will include 13 former players, during an in-person meeting in the weeks before Super Bowl 61. The 15 candidates will be reduced to 10, then 7. At that point, any candidate receiving 80% approval would be elected to the Class of 2027.

The new class will be unveiled during the NFL Honors show in Los Angeles in February.

At this point, balloting to reduce the pool of players under consideration is ongoing, with the full selection committee – reduced this year from 50 to 25 (plus 3 alternates) – engaging in multiple reduction votes in the coming weeks.

The Hall’s bylaws stipulate that between three and seven new Hall of Famers will be elected.

Time (and voting) will tell whether that class includes Belichick and Kraft.

The Bears were on their bye week, and maybe that was for the best. New Orleans is susceptible to big plays late in games, and that’s exactly where Thomas can shine.

TE Bauer Sharp

Tampa Bay was also on their bye week, but unlike Thomas, Sharp does not have to prove anything else for more playing time. The Buccaneers’ offense would be better with Sharp on the field, and with the NFC South being as bad as it is, any team can finish in first place. To make that happen for Tampa Bay, Sharp needs to play more on offense.

WR Barion Brown

Last week, we saw what happens when rookie Jordyn Tyson gets consistent snaps. Brown can’t get involved in the offense, so he needs ot make his mark on special teams instead. We really didn’t see much of that in the Panthers matchup, but the Saints will need some great returns from him this week against the Bears.

LB Harold Perkins

It’s only a matter of time before Perkins becomes the Falcons’ best defensive player. He makes play after play throughout the games, continues to perform against good teams, and is extremely consistent. He faced a really good team in the Kansas City Chiefs and met all expectations. Although it includes just one appearance since September — and only one without Jalen Hurts — Smith has cleared 6/60 in each of his past three games. Joe Milton is a potential fantasy anchor, but bye-addled lineups have to take WR2 work where they can find it. … Carnell Tate’s two-game absence weirdly coincided with the best two-game stretch of Cam Ward’s career. We are going to assume there’s not some bizarre “Ewing theory” thing going on and that Tate’s return will only enhance Ward’s improved play. Already trending toward every-week WR2 status before his interregnum, Tate is certainly a must play vs. the broken Cowboys. … Myles Price is who “we” (I don’t mean to implicate you in this) thought Reggie Virgil was? I don’t know, workshopping that one.

Now hopefully he makes like Jordyn Tyson and triples that number for his follow-up. You feel good about point chasing Downs despite his limited Week 10 work. … Keenan Allen played under 50 percent of the snaps in his 49ers debut and finished as the WR35. Not too shabby, but ... admittedly kind of shabby. I’m having a surprisingly difficult time finding a Week 11 rank I’m comfortable with, though the general takeaway is: I won’t be benching Allen in any format. … Deebo Samuel’s nuclear spiked week against the Cowboys still featured all of three catches and three targets. Coach Kyle Shanahan has an even more particular vision for Samuel’s usage this time around than he did during Deebo’s first Niners go-round. He should be a healthy part of the Week 11 game plan to counteract the Vikings’ pressure, but Samuel’s lack of floor makes him more of a WR3 than WR2.

DK Metcalf is on the WR3/4 borderline by average PPR points and must now deal with the healthy returns of Roman Wilson (finger) and Michael Pittman Jr. (foot). He has never really established a ceiling in Pittsburgh, and his floor is not what you would expect. He’s frankly a starting lineup space filler. At least that’s something that is needed for Week 11. … Emeka Egbuka has struggled to produce regardless of who is under center this season, so it’s difficult to parse how big of a deal Baker Mayfield’s return to the inactives list is going to be. Alas, everyone has struggled not to produce when facing the Lions’ pass defense this season, one now missing linchpin pass rusher Aidan Hutchinson. You aren’t working overtime to get Egbuka into your WR2 spot, but it would take some genuine effort for him to end up on Week 11 benches. ... Sunk cost Jaylen Waddle rankings will continue until morale improves. This might for real be his genuine, actual, last chance in the top 30 at wideout. He should be as healthy as he’s been in months coming off the Broncos’ bye, and the Raiders are a smash spot matchup.

If Waddle isn’t ready to operate as the Broncos’ WR1, perhaps Pat Bryant is. As is the case with Jonah Coleman, Bryant seems to pass every Sean Payton audition. He arguably has the best overall game in this strangely inert receiver corps. If you have been stashing Bryant on your bench, byemageddon is the perfect time for a pre-Thanksgiving unboxing. … You “have” to bench Jalen Coker, except, of course, you cannot actually do so this week. He has a reasonable enough “last chance” matchup in the Ravens’ increasingly broken defense. If Coker does not return to our WR2/3 graces this week, he will indeed find himself on the pine for next week’s 32-team extravaganza. … If Mark Andrews is the biggest winner of Jacoby Brissett’s insertion under center, Ja’Kobi Lane is a close second. Lane has spent most of 2026 percolating but been derailed by injuries to both himself and his quarterbacks. Now he can offer reasonable hope of being a big-play based WR4. … Malachi Fields, Elic Ayomanor and Tre’ Harris are the kind of WR4s you typically end up tiebreaking against that might actually come in handy this short-handed week. Chimere Dike also gets a second chance as a WR4/second FLEX after being handily out-produced by Ayomanor in Week 10.

RB Notes: With Kenneth Walker III (groin) set to miss a second consecutive contest, no ranking is too high for Emmett Johnson. The rookie proved his bonafides in Week 10, and the Chiefs have one of the setups of the century as two-touchdown home favorites against the Cardinals. … Bhayshul Tuten is having an ordinary season from an efficiency perspective. He is 29th in rushing success rate, in the bottom half of the league in average rush yards over expected, and has averaged more than 4.0 yards per carry just once in his past five appearances. He has nevertheless consolidated all of the work that matters in the Jaguars’ backfield, and most of the work that doesn’t. Not even the biggest summer fader like myself could contrive a way to drop him out of the top 10 as a solid road favorite against the Giants. … Tony Pollard is the RB4 by average PPR points in four games over the past five weeks. It’s been quite the fantasy save for a player who entered October looking dead in the water. He now gets an RB1 closeup with so many teams on bye and the Titans entering Jerryworld’s offensive pinball machine.

Although he’s having the season in 2026 everyone was hoping for in 2025, Bucky Irving comes with some Week 11 risk with Baker Mayfield (foot) back on the shelf. The Lions are a bad defense but hold up better against the run than the pass, while the Bucs are concerning touchdown road ‘dogs in Mayfield’s absence. You are not even considering benching Bucky, but he probably won’t be winning you your week, either. … At long last, Kyle Monangai (toe) will be active for the first time since Week 4. D’Andre Swift has stacked up fantasy points during Monangai’s seven-week absence but has been horribly inefficient while doing so. I fully expect Monangai, who has reached at least 10 carries all four times out this season, to return to enough usage to make himself FLEX useful, especially amidst this week’s byepocalypse. His return also makes Swift more of a clear RB2 than fuzzy RB1. … Jonah Coleman has been an RB1 by average PPR points since returning in Week 8. He fumbled late in Week 9, but coach Sean Payton kept him on the field. Maybe we will get one last J.K. Dobbins rug pull, but you obviously aren’t setting your Sunday lineups without Coleman in an RB2/FLEX spot.

Jonathan Taylor remained south of 70 percent of the Colts’ snaps following the trade deadline, but only just. Indy really ratcheted up the running against the Dolphins, something they will have no choice but to make a trend even as the winds turn more unfavorable for matchups like Thursday’s date with the Texans. (Indy is a massive Week 11 underdog after being favored in Week 10.) Taylor is a floor-based RB2 with little shot at one of his patented ceiling efforts … Cam Skattebo has come out the other side of several attempts to move on from him as the Giants’ bell-cow runner as a clear-cut RB2. He’s performing well in an overachieving offense, and has most of the work to himself. He has a solid floor and more upside than might initially meet the eye. … Can Derrick Henry stay alive off touchdowns? Well, he is third all time in league history with 132 rushing scores, two of which came in Week 10. At some point, Jacoby Brissett will make this a more hospitable overall offensive environment. It was actually fairly close to happening in Week 10. Henry is a solid RB2 who will probably strain for RB1 value going forward.

Coming off bye and getting healthier on offense with the major exception of quarterback, I expect the Eagles to make one more “maybe we should actually try” push before shutting things down again some time between Thanksgiving and Christmas. This is my long way of saying I don’t mind Saquon Barkley’s RB2 setup this week. … Ashton Jeanty is fourth in running back receptions (12) over the past three weeks. It is keeping him afloat in fantasy, and likely has to increase with Brock Bowers (ankle) on the shelf. Although it is devastating Jeanty never even approached durable RB1 status this season, he appears ready to limp to the finish line as a weekly starter. … There’s no daylight between Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason. They are being used as interchangeable options with clear advantages hard to come by. Frustrating, but they are at least both seeing the ball enough to provide credible FLEX returns. … Rachaad White has failed to take the bull by the horns during Jacory Croskey-Merritt’s (groin) absence. Now “Bill” has resumed practicing. Even with six teams on bye, JCM’s return would knock White out of the top 30. Bill himself would clock in somewhere in the low 30s.

The Saints seem unfamiliar with Travis Etienne’s game but they have yet to issue an apology. Etienne’s bizarre, scattershot usage has rendered him an unplayable RB2 and highly dubious FLEX option. It seems impossible to believe things can carry on in this manner, but why would you believe anything is going to change before seeing it? … Justice Hill appears poised to be one of the big winners from Jacoby Brissett’s “attempts forward” approach to quarterbacking. Hell, even the Big Dog himself, Derrick Henry, was drawing Week 10 targets. Hill has remained on the periphery of PPR FLEX value for so long that it is difficult to believe it’s finally here. Alas. … Incredibly, Tyler Allgeier continues to split snaps with journeyman Bam Knight. I am genuinely unclear how this was in the range of outcomes. I’m also unclear on what would make anything change as three-score ‘dogs vs. the Chiefs. … You are on your own beyond this point. There aren’t even Corey Kiner trapdoors to fall through this week. There simply is not enough teams playing. Maybe Audric Estime squeaks out another usable week? Maybe Emari Demercado is a thing for the Texans? Maybe, uhh, Sione Vaki for … reasons. That’s about all I got.
